text: Explain what a hash table is, why average-case lookup is constant time, and what specific condition causes that guarantee to degrade. Keep the answer to a single paragraph and do not use bullet points or code examples in your response.

Describe the difference between latency and throughput in a request-serving system. Give one concrete example of a change that improves throughput while making latency worse, and briefly explain the mechanism that produces that trade-off.

A long-running server process shows resident memory growing by about 40 megabytes per hour under steady load, and it never returns to its starting level. List the three most likely causes, and state which measurement would distinguish between them most cheaply.

Explain why floating point addition is not associative. Give a specific numeric example where changing the grouping of three values changes the result, and describe one practical consequence this has for parallel reduction operations in numerical code.

Explain the purpose of a write-ahead log in a relational database. Describe what specific failure it protects against, what ordering guarantee it must maintain to do so, and what performance cost it imposes on the commit path of a transaction.

Describe what happens when a CPU cache line is invalidated by a write from another core. Explain what false sharing is, why it degrades performance even when two threads never touch the same variable, and how it is usually fixed.

Explain why adding more worker threads to a parallel workload eventually stops improving throughput and can make it worse. Name the two distinct limits that produce this effect and describe how you would tell which one is binding in a given system.

Explain the difference between a process and a thread in terms of what each one owns and what each one shares. Describe one situation where using separate processes is clearly the better choice, and explain precisely why.

A payments service handles 4,000 requests per second at peak. Each request writes one row to a primary Postgres instance and publishes one message to a Kafka topic. The team has observed that p99 latency rises from 40 ms to 900 ms for roughly ninety seconds every hour, always starting within a minute of the top of the hour. CPU utilisation stays below 45 percent throughout. Disk write throughput shows a matching spike, and the number of active database connections roughly doubles during the affected window. The Kafka producer is configured with acks set to all and a linger time of 5 ms. Autovacuum is enabled with default settings, and the primary table receives a high volume of updates to a single indexed status column. A backup job runs at ten minutes past each hour, and a metrics rollup job runs at five minutes past.

Identify the three most likely causes of the hourly latency spike, explain the mechanism behind each one in enough detail that an engineer could act on it, and describe what single measurement you would take first to distinguish between them. State clearly what result would rule each candidate out.

A machine learning team trains a gradient boosted tree model on tabular customer data. Offline validation AUC is 0.91 and has been stable across three retraining cycles. After deployment, the production precision at a fixed threshold is consistently eight points lower than validation predicted, and the gap does not close over four weeks. The training set is assembled by a nightly batch job that joins customer events with a labels table. Labels arrive with a variable delay of between two and thirty days. The production feature service computes features at request time from a streaming store, while the training job computes the same features from a data warehouse using SQL written by a different team. Validation splitting is random rather than temporal.

Explain the most likely reason for the offline to online gap, describe how you would confirm it with a specific diagnostic, and propose a change to the training pipeline that would remove the discrepancy. Explain what you would expect the validation AUC to do after that change, and why a drop would be a sign of progress rather than regression.

Consider a distributed key-value store replicated across three data centres using a quorum protocol with a replication factor of three and both read and write quorums set to two. A network partition isolates one data centre for eleven minutes. During the partition, clients in the isolated data centre continue to issue reads and writes against their local replica, which accepts them because the client library was configured to fall back to a quorum of one when a quorum cannot be reached. When the partition heals, the system reports two hundred conflicting versions for the same set of keys, and application logs show that some users saw stale account balances during the outage.

Explain precisely which guarantee was violated and why the nominal quorum configuration did not prevent it. Describe two different conflict resolution strategies the system could apply when the partition heals, and state the specific cost that each strategy imposes on application developers. Finally, explain what the correct behaviour would have been during the partition and what the business would have had to accept in exchange.

A biologist is studying how a bacterial population develops resistance to an antibiotic. She grows twelve independent cultures from the same clonal ancestor, exposes each to a sub-lethal concentration of the drug for two hundred generations, and then sequences the survivors. Eleven of the twelve populations carry a mutation in the same efflux pump regulator gene, but each population carries a different mutation at a different position within that gene. Several of these are frameshifts and premature stop codons. The twelfth population carries no mutation in that gene and instead shows a fourfold duplication of a chromosomal region containing the drug target. All twelve populations show similar increases in minimum inhibitory concentration.

Explain what the pattern of loss-of-function mutations in eleven populations reveals about the accessibility of that resistance route compared to the duplication route. Describe what additional experiment would let her determine which route carries a higher fitness cost in the absence of the drug, and state what result would indicate that the duplication is likely to be unstable once selection is relaxed.

A central bank has held its policy rate at 5.25 percent for eleven months. Headline inflation has fallen from 9.1 percent to 3.4 percent over that period, but core services inflation remains at 5.8 percent and nominal wage growth is running at 6.2 percent against trend productivity growth of about 1 percent. Unemployment has risen from 3.7 percent to 4.3 percent, and the vacancy to unemployment ratio has fallen by a third from its peak. Long-term inflation expectations implied by the bond market are anchored near the two percent target, but household survey expectations sit at 4.5 percent. Roughly 40 percent of outstanding mortgages reprice within the next eighteen months.

Set out the strongest argument for holding the rate and the strongest argument for cutting it, giving the transmission mechanism in each case. Identify which single data series would most change your view if it moved, explain what movement would be decisive and in which direction, and state why that series carries more information than the others listed.

An engineering team is choosing between two designs for a system that ingests sensor readings from fifty thousand devices deployed in the field. Design A buffers readings in memory on each ingest node and flushes to durable storage every five seconds, acknowledging the device immediately on receipt. Design B writes every reading synchronously to a replicated log before acknowledging the device. Design A sustains roughly twelve times the throughput per node in benchmarks and costs about a fifth as much to run. The devices retry unacknowledged readings for up to one hour using exponential backoff, but they discard a reading once acknowledged. Downstream consumers compute hourly aggregates that feed into a regulatory report which the company must attest to.

Recommend one of the two designs. Your answer must state what the regulatory attestation implies about acceptable data loss, must explain precisely what would have to be true about the retry behaviour and the acknowledgement timing for the cheaper design to be defensible, and must describe a hybrid that captures most of the cost saving if that condition only partly holds.

A materials scientist is investigating why a batch of aluminium alloy components is failing fatigue testing at roughly sixty percent of the expected cycle count. The failures all originate at the same geometric feature, a fillet where a thick section meets a thin one. Metallurgical analysis shows the grain structure, composition and heat treatment response are all within specification, and tensile testing of coupons from the same batch gives yield and ultimate strength at the middle of the acceptable range. Surface roughness at the fillet measures 3.2 micrometres average, against a drawing requirement of 1.6 micrometres. Residual stress measurements at the surface show tension of 80 megapascals where the process specification calls for compression of at least 50 megapascals. The shot peening station was serviced three weeks before the batch was produced.

Explain how each of the two out-of-specification findings contributes to early fatigue crack initiation, state which one you would expect to dominate and why, and describe a process change that would address both. Explain what inspection you would add to catch a recurrence before parts reach fatigue testing.

A city is deciding whether to convert two lanes of a six-lane arterial road into a segregated bus corridor. Current traffic volume is 3,400 vehicles per hour at peak in each direction. Buses currently carry 22 percent of person trips on the corridor while occupying 4 percent of vehicle movements, and bus journey times on the corridor vary by a factor of two between free-flowing and congested conditions. Modelling commissioned by the roads department suggests general traffic delay would rise by 40 percent in the first year, assuming demand is fixed. Comparable schemes in three other cities showed total corridor traffic volumes falling by between 11 and 24 percent within two years of implementation, with no measurable increase on parallel residential routes.

Explain the mechanism that would produce the observed volume reduction in the comparator cities. State precisely what assumption the first-year delay model is making that the comparator evidence contradicts, and explain why that assumption is nonetheless reasonable for the first few months. Describe the monitoring you would put in place and what threshold would trigger reversing the scheme.

You are reviewing an incident report from a large online retailer and must produce an analysis for the engineering leadership team.

At 14:02 on a Friday, the retailer's checkout service began returning errors for approximately 3 percent of requests. The error rate climbed steadily, reaching 31 percent by 14:19, at which point an on-call engineer initiated a rollback of the most recent deployment. The rollback completed at 14:26. The error rate did not improve. At 14:34 a second engineer restarted the checkout service fleet. The error rate dropped to zero within ninety seconds and did not recur.

The deployment that was rolled back had gone out at 11:40, roughly two hours and twenty minutes before the incident began. It changed a single configuration value: the connection pool size for the inventory service client was raised from 20 to 60 per instance, across 48 checkout instances. The change was made because the team had observed connection acquisition waits during a traffic peak the previous week.

The inventory service runs on 12 instances behind a load balancer. Each instance is configured to accept a maximum of 200 concurrent connections. The inventory service holds a connection open for the duration of a request and does not use multiplexing. Inventory service CPU utilisation during the incident remained below 30 percent. Its own p99 latency, measured at the application layer, stayed under 25 milliseconds throughout. The load balancer reported a rising count of rejected connection attempts starting at 13:55, seven minutes before customer errors began.

The checkout service uses a client library configured with a connection acquisition timeout of 5 seconds and a request timeout of 30 seconds. It retries failed inventory calls up to three times with a fixed 200 millisecond delay between attempts. There is no circuit breaker. Checkout request handling is synchronous: a thread is held for the duration of the downstream call chain. The checkout service runs with a fixed thread pool of 400 threads per instance.

Traffic on the day was 18 percent above the same weekday the previous week, and had been rising gradually from 13:30 onward as a marketing email campaign landed.

Your analysis must do the following. First, explain the causal chain from the configuration change to the customer-visible errors, being specific about which resource was exhausted and where. Second, explain why the rollback at 14:26 did not resolve the incident, and why the restart at 14:34 did; your explanation must identify what state persisted across the rollback. Third, explain why the load balancer began rejecting connections at 13:55 while customer errors did not appear until 14:02, and what that seven minute gap tells you about where the queueing occurred. Fourth, identify the specific interaction between the retry policy and the exhausted resource that accelerated the failure, and quantify it approximately. Fifth, recommend three changes ranked by how much risk each removes, and for each one state what it would have done differently in this incident. Do not recommend simply reverting the pool size, and explain why that alone would be insufficient.

You are advising a research group that is designing a study to measure whether a widely used medical risk score performs differently across patient subgroups.

The risk score takes eleven clinical variables and outputs a probability that a patient admitted to hospital with chest pain will experience a major cardiac event within thirty days. It was developed twenty years ago on a cohort of approximately 12,000 patients drawn from fourteen hospitals in a single country. It is now used in emergency departments internationally to decide whether a patient is discharged, observed, or admitted for further investigation.

The group has access to a retrospective dataset of 340,000 admissions across sixty hospitals over eight years. The dataset includes all eleven score inputs, the recorded outcome at thirty days, patient age, recorded sex, a coded ethnicity field, an area-level deprivation index, the admitting hospital, and the time and date of admission. Ethnicity is missing for 19 percent of records, and the missingness is strongly correlated with the admitting hospital. Outcome data comes from linkage to a national registry and is believed to be close to complete, though linkage failure is slightly more common for patients without a stable address.

The group's initial plan is to compute the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve separately within each subgroup and to report whether the values differ. A senior clinician on the team has objected that this will not answer the question that matters clinically, which is whether the score sends patients from some groups home when it should not.

Your advice must cover the following. First, explain why comparing area under the curve across subgroups can be misleading when the outcome prevalence differs between those subgroups, and describe what quantity would better capture the clinical concern the clinician raised. Second, explain the distinction between discrimination and calibration in this setting, and describe concretely what a calibration failure would look like in the data and what harm it would cause. Third, address the missing ethnicity data: explain why a complete-case analysis would be biased here given the correlation with hospital, and describe an approach that would be more defensible along with the assumption it requires. Fourth, explain why the eight year span and the sixty hospital structure both need to be accounted for, and what would go wrong if the analysis pooled everything as independent observations. Fifth, state what result would justify recommending that the score be recalibrated rather than replaced, and what result would justify replacement. Be specific about thresholds and about what evidence would be insufficient to support either conclusion.

You are writing a technical briefing on the design of a storage engine for an engineering audience that is familiar with databases but has not worked on storage internals.

Two dominant designs exist for the on-disk structure of a key-value storage engine. The first is the B-tree, in which keys are held in a balanced tree of fixed-size pages, and a write locates the page holding the key and modifies it in place. The second is the log-structured merge tree, in which writes are appended to an in-memory table and periodically flushed to immutable sorted files on disk, with background compaction merging those files into fewer, larger ones over time.

The briefing needs to explain the consequences of this structural difference across several dimensions, and to be honest about where the answer depends on the workload rather than on the design.

Cover the following. First, explain write amplification in each design: how many times a given byte of user data is written to the physical device over its lifetime, and what drives that number in each case. Be specific about how compaction strategy affects the log-structured case, and contrast levelled compaction with size-tiered compaction. Second, explain read amplification, in particular why a point lookup in a log-structured engine may need to consult several files, what a Bloom filter does to reduce this, and what its failure mode is. Third, explain space amplification and why the two designs fail differently here, covering both page fragmentation in the B-tree case and obsolete versions awaiting compaction in the log-structured case. Fourth, explain why the log-structured design tends to produce a more variable tail latency, identify the specific mechanism responsible, and describe two techniques that reduce it. Fifth, explain how the characteristics of the underlying device change the comparison: address the difference between spinning disks and solid state drives, and explain why the internal behaviour of a solid state drive means that sequential writes are cheaper than random ones even though the device presents a flat address space.

Conclude by describing the workload profile under which each design is clearly the better choice, and identify one workload where the answer is genuinely close and explain what measurement you would take to decide. Do not present either design as universally superior.

You are preparing an analysis of an argument about historical causation for a graduate seminar.

A historian has argued that the rapid growth of a particular manufacturing region between 1780 and 1840 was caused primarily by its access to cheap coal. The evidence offered is as follows. The region sits on an exposed coalfield where seams could be worked near the surface. Coal prices at the pithead in the region were between a third and a half of prices in comparable manufacturing areas without local coal. The number of steam engines installed in the region rose from fewer than 30 in 1780 to over 1,400 by 1840. Output of finished goods rose roughly twentyfold over the same period. Regions without local coal grew more slowly on every measure the historian reports.

A second historian has challenged this account. She points out that the region also had, before 1780, an unusual concentration of skilled metalworkers, a distinctive pattern of partible inheritance that left many households with small capital sums, a navigable river connecting it to a major port, and a legal regime under which mineral rights were held separately from surface rights, which made leasing simpler than elsewhere. She notes that two other regions sat on equally accessible coalfields and did not industrialise on anything like the same scale during the period. She argues that cheap coal was necessary but that treating it as the primary cause mistakes an enabling condition for a driving one.

Your analysis must do the following. First, state precisely what claim the first historian is making, distinguishing between the claim that coal was necessary, the claim that it was sufficient, and the claim that it was the largest single contributor. Explain why these require different evidence. Second, explain what logical work the two non-industrialising coalfields do in the second historian's argument, and what the first historian would need to show about those cases to preserve the original claim. Third, identify the selection problem in comparing the region to areas without local coal, and describe what a better comparison group would look like. Fourth, explain how one would in principle separate the contribution of cheap coal from the contribution of the pre-existing skill concentration, given that both were present from the start, and be honest about whether the available historical record could support that separation. Fifth, state which of the two positions you find better supported on the evidence given, and identify the single piece of additional evidence that would most change your assessment.

You are designing the evaluation protocol for a system that will be deployed to summarise clinical consultation notes for general practitioners.

The system takes a transcript of a consultation, typically between 600 and 3,000 words, and produces a structured summary containing the presenting complaint, relevant history, examination findings, assessment, and plan. The summary is inserted into the patient record as a draft, and the clinician reviews and edits it before signing. The intended benefit is reduced documentation time. The principal risk is that a clinician signs a summary containing an error they did not notice.

You must design an evaluation that would justify deployment. The following constraints apply. Clinician time for evaluation is limited to roughly 200 hours in total. Real consultation transcripts can be used only within the provider's own infrastructure. A pilot deployment in a single practice is possible before wider rollout. The system will be compared against current practice, in which clinicians type their own notes during or after the consultation.

Your protocol must address the following. First, define the specific failure modes you are evaluating for, distinguishing at minimum between omission of clinically relevant information, inclusion of information not present in the transcript, and misattribution such as assigning a symptom to the wrong time period or the wrong person. Explain why these carry different levels of risk and why a single quality score would obscure that difference. Second, describe how you would construct an evaluation set that includes enough hard cases to be informative, and explain the sampling bias you introduce by doing so and how you would correct for it when reporting rates. Third, specify what clinicians are asked to do, how many independent reviewers each summary receives, and how you would measure and report agreement between them. Explain what level of disagreement would tell you the evaluation itself is not measuring anything stable. Fourth, explain why measuring the accuracy of the generated summary in isolation is insufficient, and describe how you would measure the property that actually matters, which is the rate of errors that survive clinician review. Explain what the pilot deployment is for and what it can measure that offline evaluation cannot. Fifth, state in advance what results would justify deployment, what results would justify deployment with restrictions, and what results would stop it. Give concrete numbers and explain the reasoning behind each threshold. Finally, describe what you would monitor after deployment and what would trigger a rollback.

You are explaining to a team of software engineers how a modern processor executes their code, in enough depth that they can reason about performance without reading assembly.

Begin with the basic pipeline. Explain what it means for an instruction to be fetched, decoded, executed and retired, and why splitting the work into stages raises throughput without reducing the latency of any individual instruction. Then explain superscalar execution: what it means for a processor to issue several instructions per cycle, and what limits how many it can actually sustain.

Move on to out-of-order execution. Explain why the processor reorders instructions, what a reservation station and a reorder buffer do, and why instructions can execute out of order while still retiring in order. Explain what the register renaming stage accomplishes and which specific class of dependency it eliminates. Distinguish clearly between true data dependencies, which no amount of hardware can remove, and false dependencies, which renaming does remove.

Then cover speculation. Explain branch prediction: why the processor must guess, what a mispredict costs in terms of discarded work, and roughly how accurate modern predictors are on typical code. Explain what makes a branch hard to predict and give a concrete code pattern that produces poor prediction, along with a rewrite that avoids the problem.

Next, cover the memory hierarchy in the same terms. Give approximate latencies in cycles for a hit in each cache level and for a main memory access, and explain why the ratio between them, rather than the absolute numbers, is what should shape how engineers write code. Explain prefetching: what patterns the hardware prefetcher recognises and what patterns defeat it. Explain why an array of structures and a structure of arrays perform differently for the same logical work, and be specific about what changes at the cache line level.

Then explain how these mechanisms interact. Explain what happens to the out-of-order window when a load misses to main memory, and why that makes memory latency partially hideable but not free. Explain why a dependent chain of pointer dereferences is one of the hardest patterns for a modern processor and what makes it different from a dependent chain of arithmetic.

Conclude with practical guidance. Give three specific things an engineer can do that follow from the above, and for each one state which mechanism it exploits. Then give one common piece of optimisation advice that is now misleading on modern hardware, and explain what changed to make it so.

You are producing a decision memo on whether an organisation should build or buy a component of its data infrastructure.

The organisation processes event data from its consumer applications: roughly 900 million events per day, growing at about 4 percent month on month. Events must be validated against a schema, enriched with reference data, deduplicated, and delivered to three destinations: a data warehouse used by analysts, a feature store used by machine learning services, and a real-time alerting system with a delivery target of under ten seconds end to end.

The current system was built in-house four years ago. It works, but the two engineers who built it have both left. It has no schema registry, so schema changes are coordinated by convention and break downstream consumers roughly once a month. Deduplication is best-effort and the warehouse team maintains their own reconciliation job to correct for it. The system cannot replay historical data without manual intervention. Adding a fourth destination is estimated at six engineer-weeks.

Two options are on the table. The first is to adopt a managed platform, at a quoted cost of roughly 480,000 per year at current volume, with pricing that scales close to linearly with event count. Migration is estimated at four engineer-months. The platform provides a schema registry, exactly-once delivery to supported destinations, and replay. Two of the three current destinations are supported natively; the feature store is not, and would need a custom connector, estimated at one engineer-month plus ongoing maintenance. The second option is a rebuild on open-source components, estimated at nine engineer-months to reach parity plus an estimated 1.5 engineers of ongoing operational load, with infrastructure costs of roughly 90,000 per year.

The organisation employs 40 engineers in total. Its stated strategy emphasises speed of product iteration. It has no dedicated platform team, and infrastructure work is currently done by whoever is free.

Your memo must do the following. First, state what the actual decision is, distinguishing it from the framing given, and explain what question the cost comparison alone fails to answer. Second, build the comparison on total cost over a defined horizon, stating your horizon and justifying it, and being explicit about which costs you are including and which you are deliberately excluding. Third, address the growth rate: explain what the linear pricing of the managed option implies at the three year point and whether that changes the recommendation. Fourth, identify the three assumptions your recommendation is most sensitive to, and for each one state how far it would have to be wrong to flip the decision. Fifth, address the organisational constraint directly: explain what the absence of a platform team implies about the realism of the 1.5 engineer ongoing estimate. Finally, give a clear recommendation and describe a decision point at which you would revisit it.

You are writing the methods critique section of a review of a submitted research paper.

The paper reports that a new training technique improves the performance of language models on reasoning benchmarks. The claimed result is an average improvement of 4.2 percentage points across six benchmarks, relative to a baseline trained without the technique.

The reported methodology is as follows. The authors trained two models, one with the technique and one without, both starting from the same public base model. Each was trained for 3,000 steps on the same dataset. Hyperparameters were tuned for the treatment model by running fourteen configurations and selecting the best by validation performance; the baseline used the hyperparameters reported in the original paper for the base model. Evaluation used six benchmarks, five of which are multiple choice and one of which is free-form generation scored by exact match. Each benchmark was evaluated once, with greedy decoding. The paper reports the mean across the six benchmarks and notes that the technique improved results on five of the six. No confidence intervals or variance estimates are reported. The paper states that the evaluation prompts were adjusted for the treatment model to better elicit the intended behaviour.

The authors also report a compute comparison, stating that the technique adds only 7 percent to training cost. This figure counts the treatment run only and does not include the hyperparameter search.

Your critique must identify the methodological problems in order of how much they threaten the central claim, and for each one explain concretely how it could produce the reported result in the absence of any real effect. Cover at minimum the asymmetric hyperparameter tuning, the prompt adjustment, the single evaluation run with no variance estimate, the choice to report a mean across benchmarks with different scales and difficulty, and the compute accounting.

For each problem, state specifically what additional experiment or reporting would resolve it, and be realistic about cost. Distinguish clearly between problems that make the result uninterpretable and problems that merely weaken it. State what the minimum acceptable revision would be for the paper to support its central claim, and state separately whether you believe the claim is likely to be true, explaining why that judgement is independent of whether the paper currently establishes it.
